specPoints.text: understand the advantages and disadvantages of using stem cells in medicine

primer.text: Stem cells are the body's undifferentiated reserve — cells that can keep dividing or become specialised. This note separates adult from embryonic stem cells, then weighs the medical promise against the risks and the ethics: bone-marrow transplants that save blood patients, rejection dangers, and the embryo debate that examiners love as an evaluation question.

lessons.title: The undifferentiated toolkit: adult versus embryonic
lessons.opening: A stem cell is an undifferentiated cell that can divide by mitosis again and again, and its daughter cells may stay undifferentiated or specialise. Adult stem cells sit in tissues such as bone marrow and can differentiate into a limited range; embryonic stem cells, found only in embryos, can differentiate into any cell type the body needs.
keyPoints: A stem cell is an undifferentiated cell that can divide by mitosis to self-renew or specialise.
Daughter cells of a stem cell division may stay undifferentiated or become specialised.
Adult stem cells live in tissues such as bone marrow and differentiate into a limited range of types.
Embryonic stem cells exist only in embryos and can differentiate into any cell type.

low.restatement: Stem cells = undifferentiated, mitosis-capable. Adult: limited range, in tissues like marrow. Embryonic: any type, embryos only.
low.analogy: Adult stem cells are a trade apprentice trained for one guild; embryonic stem cells are a fresh school leaver who could join any guild at all.
low.examPointer: 'Limited range' versus 'any type' is the contrast that scores the adult-versus-embryonic comparison.

medium.restatement: Potency is the organising variable: adult stem cells carry partial potency tied to their tissue, embryonic stem cells are effectively pluripotent, and both self-renew through mitosis before committing.
medium.analogy: Two kinds of blank keys: one cut to open a few doors in one building, one still blank enough for any lock in town.
medium.examPointer: Therapy questions hinge on potency: the embryonic advantage IS the wider differentiation range.

check.stem: Which statement describes an undifferentiated, mitosis-capable cell?

options.text: An undifferentiated cell able to divide by mitosis and produce specialised descendants
options.explanation: Undifferentiated plus mitosis plus specialisation potential.

options.text: A fully specialised cell that repairs tissue
options.explanation: Specialised cells are the opposite of stem cells.

options.text: Any cell found in bone marrow
A cell that has stopped dividing

check.stem: When a stem cell divides, what can its daughters become?

options.text: They merge into one larger cell
They may stay undifferentiated or specialise into particular cell types
They always become specialised immediately
They always remain stem cells

check.stem: Which statement contrasts adult and embryonic stem cells correctly?

options.text: Embryonic stem cells are found in bone marrow
Both types exist only in embryos
options.explanation: Adult stem cells live in tissues.

options.text: Embryonic stem cells can differentiate into any cell type; adult ones into a limited range
options.explanation: Potency difference is the named contrast.

options.text: Adult stem cells can become any cell type

check.stem: Where are adult stem cells found, according to the note?

options.text: Only in embryos
Floating freely in the blood
Nowhere after birth
In some tissues and organs, for example the bone marrow
options.explanation: The named location with its example.

check.stem: Why are embryonic stem cells prized for therapy despite the ethics?

options.text: Because their wider differentiation range lets them become whichever tissue a treatment needs
Because they multiply faster than bacteria
Because they avoid all immune rejection
Because they are the only undifferentiated cells

check.stem: State the word for a cell that has not yet specialised.
Name the process by which stem cells divide.
check.modelAnswer: Mitosis — the division route stem cells use.

check.stem: Explain why bone marrow counts as a stem-cell niche even though blood cells are constantly made there.
check.modelAnswer: Bone marrow hosts adult stem cells that keep dividing by mitosis, feeding the constant production of blood cells; the tissue's ability to restock red cells, white cells and platelets is exactly the self-renewal-plus-specialisation behaviour that defines a stem-cell population.

check.stem: A lab brochure claims its cell line 'can become any human cell type'. Which stem-cell class does that describe, and where must the line have come from?
check.modelAnswer: Any-type potency describes embryonic stem cells, so the line must have originated from embryonic tissue rather than from an adult tissue such as bone marrow.

lessons.title: Stem cells in medicine: promise, rejection and ethics
sourceHeadings: Evaluating Stem Cells in Medicine Table
lessons.opening: Medicine wants stem cells where the body's own cells fail. Bone-marrow transplants show the promise — donor marrow rebuilds a patient's red cells, white cells and platelets — but donor antigens can trigger rejection, so a patient's own cells are safer. Embryonic sources add an ethical dimension: growing embryos for harvesting troubles people who see embryos as human life.
keyPoints: Stem cells could treat illnesses where the body's own cells no longer function properly.
Bone-marrow transplants rebuild blood: red cells for anaemia, white cells for immunity, platelets for clotting.
Donor cells carry different antigens, so the patient's immune system may reject them.
A patient's own stem cells avoid rejection and the need for immunosuppressant drugs.
Growing embryos as an embryonic-stem-cell source raises ethical objections for some people.

low.restatement: Promise: rebuild failing tissue (marrow for blood). Risk: donor antigen rejection. Ethics: embryo use. Own cells beat donor cells on safety.
low.analogy: A transplant is a spare-parts order: the best part is your own (no fitting problems), a donor's may not fit, and the embryonic catalogue raises arguments of its own.
low.examPointer: Evaluation answers need BOTH sides plus a conclusion — benefit, risk/ethics, then a judgement.

medium.restatement: The evaluation is a trade-off triangle: therapeutic potency (embryonic best), immune compatibility (own cells best), and ethical cost (embryonic worst) — the bone-marrow case sits at the compatible-but-limited corner.
medium.analogy: Choosing stem cells is like choosing a organ donor list policy: capability, compatibility and consent pull in different directions.
medium.examPointer: Name immunosuppressant drugs explicitly when contrasting donor and patient-own cells.

check.stem: Which blood products does a bone-marrow transplant restore?

options.text: Red cells, white cells and platelets
Red cells only
Platelets only
Plasma proteins only

check.stem: Why might a patient's immune system reject donor bone-marrow cells?

options.text: Because marrow cells lack haemoglobin
The donor cells carry different surface antigens from the patient's own
options.explanation: Antigen difference is the named trigger.

options.text: Because donor cells are larger
Because donor cells cannot divide

check.stem: What advantage do a patient's OWN stem cells have over donor cells?

options.text: They are free of ethical objections always
options.explanation: Ethics depends on the source, and adult autologous cells are the uncontroversial case.

options.text: They divide faster than embryonic cells
No rejection and no immunosuppressant drugs needed
They can become any cell type

check.stem: Which illness is treated with red blood cells from marrow-derived stem cells?

options.text: Pneumonia
options.explanation: That is a bacterial lung infection.

options.text: Malaria
Diabetes
Anaemia — the blood cannot carry enough oxygen

check.stem: What is the ethical objection some people raise about embryonic stem cells?

options.text: Growing human embryos as a source treats embryos as potential human life to be harvested
options.explanation: The embryo-status concern is the named objection.

options.text: Embryonic cells are expensive to freeze
options.explanation: Cost is not the named objection.

options.text: Embryos divide too slowly
Embryonic cells cannot specialise

check.stem: Name the surface proteins whose difference triggers rejection of donor cells.
check.modelAnswer: Antigens — the surface proteins that mark cell identity.

check.stem: Name the drugs a patient takes to prevent immune rejection of donor cells.
Explain why white-cell transfusions from marrow-derived stem cells help patients with weakened immune systems.
check.modelAnswer: White cells such as phagocytes and lymphocytes are the immune system's working cells; a patient with a reduced immune system lacks them, so marrow-derived white cells restore pathogen-fighting capacity directly.

check.stem: A hospital must choose between donor marrow and the patient's own marrow cells for a transplant. Using this note, state which is safer and give the two-part reason.
check.modelAnswer: The patient's own marrow cells are safer: they carry the patient's own antigens, so no immune rejection occurs, and the patient avoids immunosuppressant drugs with their infection risks.

glossary.definition: A stem cell found only in embryos, able to differentiate into any cell type.
A protein on the cell surface whose difference between donor and patient can trigger rejection.
The tissue inside bones where adult stem cells make blood cells.
